title: Chappar Chiri, 1710
hookLine: at Chappar Chiri Banda's forces defeat Wazir Khan, the governor who ordered the Sahibzade's deaths

lines: THE GOVERNOR WHO GAVE THE ORDER.
cards: Go back, for a moment, to a cold tower in Sirhind.
Earlier on this path you sat with Mata Gujri and the Guru's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, held there in the winter, and with the order that ended the boys' lives.
The man who gave that order was the governor of Sirhind, Wazir Khan, and Sikh memory kept his name.
Now the story arrives at a stretch of open ground outside Sirhind called Chappar Chiri, where Banda Singh's army and Wazir Khan's forces meet.

teach.h: A HARD FIGHT ON AN OPEN FIELD.
teach.b: Sikh tellings describe a hard fight on that field. Tradition remembers Banda Singh's army as farmers and villagers as much as soldiers, facing a well-armed governor's force.

teach.h: WAZIR KHAN FALLS; SIRHIND IS TAKEN.
teach.b: By the end of the day, tradition says, Wazir Khan had fallen, and Sirhind itself was taken after. So the line is two plain words: it came. The answer to that winter order finally came.
But listen to what Sikhs say when they greet each other: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh.
The Khalsa belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory. Fateh means victory, and it's also the name of the youngest of those two boys in the tower, Fateh Singh.
In the Sikh way of saying it, the victory on the field doesn't belong to Banda Singh. It belongs to Waheguru.

teach.h: AN ENDING DOESN'T GIVE BACK THE LOST.
teach.b: And it doesn't give anything back. No battle gives back two boys, or the grandmother who died beside them.
That's why the line is it came, and not we won. An ending arrived. It closed one long wait.
It didn't erase what was lost. This also closes a week that began with far-off sangats, the letters that kept them close, and a last look at the people around the Gurus.
Then a hermit at Nanded became a servant, carried five arrows north, and faced the question of justice at Samana. Today the long wait for Sirhind reaches its end.

how: Sikhs remember the battle of Chappar Chiri and the taking of Sirhind as the end of Wazir Khan, who ordered the deaths of the younger Sahibzade, and greet one another with the words that the victory belongs to Waheguru.

games.q: the governor who gave the order has fallen and the city is taken. how does the Sikh greeting name the victory?
games.why: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh: the Khalsa and the victory both belong to Waheguru.

practice: Think of something you waited a long time for, a diagnosis, an apology, a verdict, a letter, and remember the moment it finally came.

Notice what it gave you, and honestly what it couldn't give back, and let both sit side by side without choosing. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, and let the ending belong to something bigger than you.

wordCard.voice: Chappar Chiri. The field near Sirhind where, in Sikh tradition, Banda Singh's army met the forces of Wazir Khan, who fell there.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: fateh, victory, as in Waheguru ji ki Fateh; also the name of Guru Gobind Singh's youngest son.
